q: How does a decision tree make a prediction?
short: It routes an example from the root through attribute tests to a leaf, and outputs that leaf's class (or value).
detail: Each path is a conjunction of conditions; the tree is a disjunction of paths. Prediction cost is O(depth).

q: What is entropy?
short: The expected information (uncertainty) of a class distribution: H = −Σ p log₂ p.
detail: 0 for a pure set, 1 bit for a 50/50 binary set, up to log₂ k for k classes.
mistakes: Saying entropy can exceed 1 for two classes.

q: What is information gain?
short: The reduction in entropy from splitting on an attribute: H(S) − Σ |Sv|/|S| H(Sv).
detail: ID3 picks the attribute with the highest gain at each node.

q: Describe the ID3 algorithm.
short: Greedy top-down: pick the best-gain attribute, split, recurse on each branch with remaining attributes, stop when pure or out of attributes.
detail: Leaves get the majority class when attributes run out; empty branches get the parent's majority.
mistakes: Reusing an attribute already on the path (for categorical).

q: Entropy vs Gini index?
short: Both measure impurity and are 0 for pure nodes; Gini = 1 − Σ p², entropy = −Σ p log p.
detail: Gini is cheaper (no logs) and is CART's default; they usually pick the same splits.

q: Why do decision trees overfit?
short: They can keep splitting until every training point is isolated, fitting noise.
detail: Deep trees have low bias, high variance. Training error → 0 while test error rises.
example: Slides: 50-node tree carving boxes around noise.

q: Pre-pruning vs post-pruning?
short: Pre-pruning stops growth early (gain threshold, max depth, min samples); post-pruning grows fully, then removes branches that don't help on a validation set.
detail: Pre-pruning is cheaper but can stop too early (horizon effect); post-pruning usually generalises better.
mistakes: Using training error to decide pruning.

q: How are continuous attributes handled?
short: Convert to binary tests A ≤ c, choosing c among midpoints of sorted values that minimise impurity.
detail: Candidates only need to be where the class changes. Slides: income ≤ 97.5K minimises Gini (0.300).
follow: Can the same attribute be reused deeper?
mistakes: Testing every observed value instead of midpoints.

q: What are the main advantages of decision trees?
short: Interpretable, fast, little preprocessing (no scaling), handle mixed types and irrelevant features.
detail: They are also non-parametric and capture interactions through nested splits.
example: Credit rules a regulator can read.

q: What is gain ratio?
short: Information gain divided by split information (entropy of the partition sizes); it penalises attributes with many values.
detail: SplitInfo = −Σ |Si|/|S| log₂ |Si|/|S|. Customer ID: gain 1, SplitInfo 4.32, ratio 0.23 < Car type 0.41.
mistakes: Assuming highest gain is always best.

q: Compute Gain(S, Wind) for PlayTennis.
Why is information gain biased toward many-valued attributes?
short: Splitting into many small subsets makes each nearly pure, lowering weighted entropy without generalising.
detail: Extreme case: an ID column gives singletons with zero entropy. Gain ratio or binary splits counteract this.
mistakes: Using IDs or timestamps as features.

q: Explain the Gini computation for the Home Owner split.
short: Parent Gini 0.420; children: Yes [0, 3] → 0, No [3, 4] → 0.490; weighted 0.343; gain 0.077.
detail: Gini(t) = 1 − Σ p²; weight children by N(v)/N.
follow: Which marital split ties with it?
mistakes: Weighting equally instead of by size.

q: Your tree has 100% training accuracy and 70% test accuracy. What do you do?
short: Control complexity: limit depth/leaves, set min samples per leaf, or prune with cost-complexity tuned by cross-validation; consider ensembles.
detail: Check for leakage too. Plot validation error vs complexity and choose the minimum.

q: How does post-pruning with a prune set work?
short: Bottom-up, replace each subtree with its majority leaf if that doesn't increase error on a separate prune (validation) set.
detail: Repeat until no further improvement. Reduced-error pruning is simple and effective given enough data.

q: What is the MDL principle?
short: Choose the hypothesis minimising bits to encode the model plus bits to encode the data's exceptions given the model.
detail: It equals MAP: −log P(h) − log P(D|h). Trades tree size for training errors (Occam's razor).
example: Tree (a) 14 + 7 log₂ n vs (b) 26 + 4 log₂ n.
mistakes: Thinking MDL always picks the smallest tree.

q: Implement entropy and information gain in Python.
short: Use class proportions; weight child entropies by size.
detail:
def H(y):
    p = y.value_counts(normalize=True)
    return -(p * np.log2(p)).sum()

def gain(df, a, t='Play'):
    w = df[a].value_counts(normalize=True)
    return H(df[t]) - sum(w[v] * H(df[df[a] == v][t]) for v in w.index)
mistakes: Using log base e and comparing to slides.

q: Multi-way vs binary splits?
short: Multi-way creates one branch per value (ID3/C4.5); binary splits into two groups (CART).
detail: Binary splits avoid fragmenting data and the many-values bias but may need more depth; ordinal splits must respect order.
follow: How many binary partitions of k categories exist?
mistakes: Splitting ordinal values out of order.

q: Why are decision boundaries axis-parallel, and why does it matter?
short: Each test uses one attribute against a threshold, so regions are rectangles.
detail: Diagonal boundaries need many small steps (deep trees). Oblique trees or feature engineering (x₁ − x₂) help.
example: Linear boundary approximated by a staircase.
mistakes: Assuming trees capture any boundary cheaply.

q: How would you choose between entropy and Gini in practice?
short: Try both via cross-validation; differences are usually small; Gini is faster.
detail: Hyperparameters like depth, min_samples_leaf and ccp_alpha matter far more.
mistakes: Spending effort on criterion before depth.

q: What is the computational complexity of building a CART tree?
short: About O(d · n log n) per level with pre-sorting, so roughly O(d n log² n) for a balanced tree.
detail: Each node scans sorted values per feature; histogram methods (LightGBM) reduce this to O(d · bins).

q: Explain cost-complexity pruning.
short: Minimise R(T) + α|leaves(T)|; increasing α gives a nested sequence of pruned trees; pick α by validation.
detail: Weakest-link pruning removes the subtree with the smallest increase in error per removed leaf.

q: Show MDL equals MAP.
short: MAP maximises P(D|h)P(h) ⇔ minimises −log₂P(D|h) − log₂P(h); with optimal codes these are L(D|h) + L(h).
detail: Optimal code length for probability p is −log₂ p (Shannon).
follow: What does the choice of code imply?
mistakes: Treating MDL as unrelated to Bayes.

q: Why are single trees high-variance and how do ensembles fix it?
short: Small data changes alter early splits, cascading into different trees; averaging many decorrelated trees reduces variance.
detail: Bagging and random forests average; boosting reduces bias sequentially (Module 9).
example: Random forest on the same data.
follow: Why do random forests subsample features?

q: How do trees handle missing values?
short: Options: send to the most common branch, fractional instances (C4.5), surrogate splits (CART), or learn a default direction (XGBoost).
detail: Missingness can be informative; an explicit indicator may help.
follow: How does XGBoost learn the default direction?

q: Is impurity-based feature importance reliable?
short: It is biased toward high-cardinality or continuous features and computed on training data.
detail: Permutation importance on validation data or SHAP values are more reliable.

q: Decision tree vs logistic regression?
short: Trees capture non-linearity and interactions, need no scaling, but are unstable and axis-aligned; LR is stable, calibrated, linear in features.
detail: On small tabular data both are good baselines; ensembles of trees usually win on complex tabular data.
follow: When would LR beat a tree?

q: Your tree's root changes when you add 2% more data. Should you worry?
short: Yes for interpretability; it shows high variance. Use ensembles for accuracy, or stabilise with pruning and min_samples_leaf.
detail: Report stability (e.g. across bootstraps) if the tree is used for explanation.

q: Prove the maximum entropy for k classes is log₂ k.
short: By Jensen's inequality on the concave log, Σ p log(1/p) ≤ log Σ p·(1/p) = log k, with equality at uniform p.
detail: Hence 0 ≤ H ≤ log₂ k; slides note the binary range 0–1.
mistakes: Claiming entropy is bounded by 1 for any k.

q: How do regression trees differ from classification trees?
short: Leaves predict the mean target; splits minimise variance (MSE) instead of impurity.
detail: Same greedy growth and pruning; outputs are piecewise constant and can't extrapolate.
follow: How does gradient boosting use regression trees?
